ety.text: From Middle English hyve, from Old English hȳf, from Proto-West Germanic *hūfi, from Proto-Indo-European *kuHp- (“water vessel”), from *kew- (“to bend, curve”). See also Dutch huif (“beehive”), Danish dialect huv (“ship’s hull”); also Latin cūpa (“tub, vat”), Ancient Greek κύπη (kúpē, “gap, hole”), κύπελλον (kúpellon, “beaker”), Sanskrit कूप (kū́pa, “cave”). Doublet of coupe, cup, and keeve. The computing term was chosen as an in-joke relating to bees; see this for more.

senses.d: A structure, whether artificial or natural, for housing a swarm of honeybees.
The bees of one hive; a swarm of bees.
ex: When that the general is not like the hive, to whom the foragers shall all repair, what honey is expected?

senses.d: A place swarming with busy occupants; a crowd.
ex: There the horde of Roman robbers mock at a barbarous adversary. / There the hive of Roman liars worship a gluttonous emperor-idiot.
Windows builds the registry from the five registry hives[…]
to hive a swarm of bees

senses.d: To store (something other than bees) in, or as if in, a hive.
ex: Hiving wisdom with each studious year.

senses.d: To take lodging or shelter together; to reside in a collective body.
ex:
1725, Alexander Pope, letter to Martha Blount
[…] to get into warmer houses, and hive together in cities

senses.d: Of insects: to enter or possess a hive.
An itchy, red, swollen area of the skin; singular or attributive form of hives.
ex: Itchy, hive-like bumps turn into solid knotlike eruptions, which can last from a few days to several months.
[She had an] itchy hive reaction on her chest—it always seemed to happen when she talked to her mother.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish ensamne (“swarm, beehive”), from Latin exāminem, singular accusative of exāmen (“swarm”). Doublet of examen, which was borrowed.
